newsitem.title: EGYPT: Cool reception awaits Israel's Netanyahu in Cairo.
newsitem.headline: Cool reception awaits Israel's Netanyahu in Cairo.

text.p: A cool reception awaits Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when he comes to Cairo on Wednesday on his second trip to the largest Arab country and the first to make peace with the Jewish state.

Diplomats in Cairo expect Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to avoid any overt confrontation with Netanyahu but he will not hide Egyptian exasperation with Israeli policies, especially plans to build more houses for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem.

Many Egyptians outside the government are hostile to the very concept of the visit though others are willing to give Mubarak the benefit of the doubt when he decided it was better to give Netanyahu a piece of his mind than to ostracise him.
Even before the two men meet, commentators are predicting the usually sanguine and stoic Egyptian president will be candid, the diplomatic euphemism for directly critical.

"In Cairo the Israeli prime minister will hear nothing but the truth for the sake of peace and stability. President Mubarak will as usual be frank with him and sincere in expressing his point of view," said the government newspaper al-Akhbar.

"But I wouldn't expect any fireworks," added one diplomat. "Mubarak doesn't want to complicate his visit to Washington next week." The president will leave for the United States on March 8 on his first visit since President Bill Clinton's re-election.

Mubarak said on Monday he would again tell Netanyahu that progress towards Middle East peace could be at risk after the Israeli government approved last week a plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on part of West Bank Israel captured in 1967.
The affair has set back the improvement in Israeli-Egyptian relations that followed Israel and the Palestinians signing an agreement in January on the town of Hebron.

Mubarak first met the Israeli leader last July but he later accused Netanyahu of reneging on promises made on that occasion. He refused to meet Netanyahu again until he came to terms on the Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town. The two leaders saw each other a month ago in the Swiss resort of Davos but without signs of warmth.
In an interview with the New York Times this week, Mubarak said he still could not make his first official visit to Israel because Egyptian public opinion would be hostile.
Outside government circles, the loudest voices in Egypt certainly oppose even Netanyahu's visit, seen as a lesser evil than Mubarak setting foot in the Jewish state.
The main leftist party, the Tagamma, said Cairo should not receive Netanyahu while his government is planning settlements, bombing south Lebanon and refusing to return the Golan Heights.
"Our party calls on the Egyptian people to reject this visit. In their name it says 'No welcome to Netanyahu, the enemy of peace and the enemy of the Arabs'," said a party statement.
The Nasserite party is also against the visit. Party leader Ziauddin Dawoud told the international newspaper al-Hayat he wanted all Egyptians to boycott the visit.
One commentator from the liberal Wafd party said that under present conditions the visit was a mistake by any criteria.

"In the end it will do more harm than good by giving the world the impression that Cairo...is opening its arms to the Israeli prime minister after all he has said and done and that what he advocates is open to discussion," he said.
After meeting Mubarak, Netanyahu faces a second test when he meets a delegation of Egyptian businessmen. Israeli officials will be watching closely to see who dares turn up.
